1.note: The author is using **all that he had killed** as a common expression of his culture to mean “all about how he had killed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and all about how he had killed]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:40. Alternate translation: [and had had the people kill]

2.q: כֹּֽה־יַעֲשׂ֤וּ⁠ן אֱלֹהִים֙ וְ⁠כֹ֣ה יוֹסִפ֔וּ⁠ן כִּֽי־כָ⁠עֵ֤ת מָחָר֙ אָשִׂ֣ים אֶֽת־נַפְשְׁ⁠ךָ֔ כְּ⁠נֶ֖פֶשׁ אַחַ֥ד מֵ⁠הֶֽם
2.note: Following the custom of this culture, Jezebel is swearing an oath by stating a condition and the consequence she is asking the gods to make happen if the condition is met. She is stating the consequence before the condition. If it would be helpful to your readers, in your translation, you could state the condition before the consequence. Alternate translation: [Unless I have made your life like the life of one from them by this time tomorrow, thus may the gods do, and thus may they add]
See how you translated the similar expression “and thus may he add” in 2:23. Alternate translation: [and may they do even worse]

3.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “And he saw.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “And he was afraid.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

The author is speaking as if Elijah actually **saw** something. He means that Elijah realized something. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he saw how things stood] or [And he realized what would happen if he stayed in Israel]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:40. Alternate translation: [and he took action]

The author is using **went for his life** as a common expression of his culture to mean “fled to save his life” or “ran away to avoid being killed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and ran for his life] or [and fled for safety]

The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. He is specifying that Beersheba was within the kingdom of **Judah**, not within Jezebel’s kingdom of Israel, to help readers understand that Elijah knew his servant would be safe if he left him there. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

4.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:8. Alternate translation: [And for his part, he went]

Elijah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of despair and exhaustion. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what Elijah was feeling, or you could say what made him feel despair and exhaustion. Alternate translation: [I am as tired and discouraged as I can bear]

4.q: עַתָּ֤ה יְהוָה֙ קַ֣ח נַפְשִׁ֔⁠י כִּֽי־לֹא־ט֥וֹב אָנֹכִ֖י מֵ⁠אֲבֹתָֽ⁠י
4.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [since I am not better than my fathers, take my life]

Elijah could be using the term **fathers** to mean: (1) his ancestors. Since they have died, he accepts that a time will come for him to die too, and it may as well be now. Alternate translation: [I do not need to keep living; after all, my ancestors have all died] or (2) the prophets who came before him, who had not gotten the people of Israel to worship Yahweh any more than he apparently had. (In 2 Kings 2:12, Elisha calls Elijah “my father,” suggesting that this was a term that prophets used to describe their predecessors.) Alternate translation: [I have been no more successful than the prophets who came before me]

5.note: See how you translated the comparable expression “behold” in 18:7, where it similarly indicates that something happened suddenly. Alternate translation: [And suddenly an angel was touching him]

6.note: In this context, the author is using the term **behold** to focus the attention of his audience on what he is about to say. See how you translated the similar expression in 1:14.

The author is using the possessive form to describe a **bread-cake** that someone, probably the angel, had baked on **hot stones**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [was a bread-cake baked on hot stones]

The phrase **returned and lay down** expresses a single idea. The word **returned** indicates in what way Elijah **lay down**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [and he lay down again]

7.note: It might seem that the expression **returned a second time** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And the angel of Yahweh returned] or [And the angel of Yahweh came a second time]

7.q: ק֣וּם אֱכֹ֑ל כִּ֛י רַ֥ב מִמְּ⁠ךָ֖ הַ⁠דָּֽרֶךְ
7.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since the journey will be too much for you, arise, eat!]

The angel means that the journey will require more strength than Elijah has if he does not eat something more. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the journey will be too much for you if you do not eat something more]

9.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 6:11. Alternate translation: [Yahweh spoke a message to him]

Yahweh is using **What to you here** as a common expression of his culture to mean “What are you doing here?” or “Why have you come here?” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What are you doing here] or [Why have you come here]

10.q: קַנֹּ֨א קִנֵּ֜אתִי לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה ׀ אֱלֹהֵ֣י צְבָא֗וֹת כִּֽי־עָזְב֤וּ בְרִֽיתְ⁠ךָ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתֶ֣י⁠ךָ הָרָ֔סוּ וְ⁠אֶת־נְבִיאֶ֖י⁠ךָ הָרְג֣וּ בֶ⁠חָ֑רֶב
10.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because the sons of Israel have forsaken your covenant, torn down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword, being jealous, I have been jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies]

Elijah is repeating forms of a verb that means “to be jealous” in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I have been very jealous]

Even though Elijah is speaking to Yahweh directly, he is speaking of him in the third person to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this with a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [you, Yahweh]
See how you translated the similar expression in [6:1](ta:06). Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

Elijah is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I am left** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he feeling isolated. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And I am the only one who is left]

11.q: צֵ֣א וְ⁠עָמַדְתָּ֣ בָ⁠הָר֮ לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָה֒ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֧ה יְהוָ֣ה עֹבֵ֗ר וְ⁠ר֣וּחַ גְּדוֹלָ֡ה וְ⁠חָזָ֞ק
11.note: The direct quotation from Yahweh may continue through the expression **passing by**. Alternate translation: [“Go out, and you shall stand on the mountain to the face of Yahweh, for behold, Yahweh will be passing by.” And a great and strong wind]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of Yahweh]

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person, probably because he is giving an authoritative command. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [in my presence]

The terms **great** and **strong** mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a very strong wind]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of Yahweh] or [as Yahweh approached]

12.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **stillness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [there was a still, small voice] or [there was a soft, quiet voice]

13.note: Wrapping his face in his cloak was a symbolic action by which Elijah showed reverence and humility before God. He did not consider himself holy enough or worthy enough to look directly at Yahweh while Yahweh was speaking to him. (At the burning bush, Moses similarly hid his face and did not look at God, Exodus 3:6.) If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [that he reverently covered his face with his cloak]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:9. Alternate translation: [What are you doing here] or [Why have you come here]

14.note: What Elijah says here is identical to what he says in verse 10. See how you translated this expression and the rest of this statement there. Alternate translation: [I have been very jealous]

17.note: Here, the **sword** of a person represents their attempt to kill someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from Hazael’s attempt to kill him … from Jehu’s attempt to kill him]

18.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [7,000 people]

This may be a rounded or symbolic number. It was conventional in this culture to use the number seven and multiples of ten to indicate completeness. However, rather than represent the number **7,000** in your translation with a phrase such as “a full number of people,” we recommend that you express the number and explain its possible symbolic meaning in a footnote.

18.q: כָּל־הַ⁠בִּרְכַּ֗יִם אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא־כָֽרְעוּ֙ לַ⁠בַּ֔עַל וְ⁠כָ֨ל־הַ⁠פֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־נָשַׁ֖ק לֽ⁠וֹ
18.note: Yahweh is using part of people, their **knees** and **mouth**, to represent all of them in the action of remaining faithful to him and not worshiping Baal. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of the people who have not bowed their knees to Baal and everyone who has not kissed him with his mouth]

18.q: כָּל־הַ⁠בִּרְכַּ֗יִם אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא־כָֽרְעוּ֙ לַ⁠בַּ֔עַל וְ⁠כָ֨ל־הַ⁠פֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־נָשַׁ֖ק לֽ⁠וֹ
18.note: When people **bowed** to Baal and **kissed** his statue, these were symbolic actions by which they were expressing worship and devotion to Baal. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [all of the people who have not bowed down to worship Baal and everyone who has not kissed his statue as an act of devotion]

19.note: The author is using one person who was involved in this **plowing**, Elisha, to represent him and everyone else who was involved. The context suggests that the others were servants and Elisha was directing them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he was directing the plowing]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [with 12 pairs of oxen]

Here, **to his face** represents the other people who were plowing being in front of Elisha, where he could see them and supervise them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of him] or [under his supervision]

When Elijah **threw his cloak** on Elisha, this was a symbolic action by which he showed that he was appointing Elisha to be his successor as a prophet. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he threw his cloak on him to show that he was appointing him as his successor]

20.note: Elisha is using one action that would be part of a ceremonial goodbye, a **kiss**, to represent the entire action of saying a proper goodbye to his parents. (The context shows that this involved a ceremonial meal.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let me say a proper goodbye to my father and my mother]
Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [Go, return. After all,]

Elijah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I have done nothing to you that would prevent that]

21.note: The implication is that Elisha used the wooden plowing **equipment** to make a fire, on which he could put a pot of water and boil the meat from the oxen. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with the equipment of the oxen he made a fire and boiled them]

The author is first indicating generally that Elisha boiled the oxen, and he is then indicating specifically what part of them he boiled. It may be natural in your language to use a possessive form here. Alternate translation: [their flesh]
